name: Street Custom 'Gutter Psalm' Reclaimed Pipe Shotgun
description: A single-shot break-action shotgun fabricated from reclaimed industrial pipe, a door hinge, and whatever firing mechanism the builder had on hand. The Gutter Psalm pattern has proliferated across GLMZ's lower tiers through hand-copied fabrication sheets passed between squatter communities. Each one is unique but follows the same basic geometry — a length of Schedule 40 pipe, a crude breech block, and a striker fashioned from a nail or bolt. They are dangerously unreliable, occasionally lethal to the operator, and absolutely everywhere.
specifications:
gauge: variable, accepts most 12-gauge shells with shimming
capacity: 1 round
effective range: 2-8 meters
weight: 1.5-3 kg depending on pipe stock
failure rate: estimated 1 in 40 firings results in breech rupture
story_hooks: A community organizer in Tier 1 has been distributing improved Gutter Psalm schematics with better breech designs — someone wants to know who is arming the lower tiers.
A rash of breech rupture injuries at a free clinic all trace back to a single batch of defective pipe stock deliberately introduced into the supply chain.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutally utilitarian tube gun that looks assembled from industrial salvage. The silhouette is unmistakably crude—a length of weathered pipe with a misaligned breech block welded or bolted perpendicular, topped by a striker assembly that resembles jury-rigged hardware more than a firing mechanism. It reads as dangerous improvisation rather than manufactured intent.
physical_description.dimensions: Barrel: 35-45 cm, Overall length: 50-62 cm, Bore diameter: 18-19 mm (12-gauge), Breech assembly depth: 8-12 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and front-heavy, with a dead-weight feel—the pipe holds inertia poorly balanced against the crude stock. Typically 1.5-3 kg depending on the specific salvage used, making it fatiguing to aim for extended periods.
physical_description.primary_material: Schedule 40 industrial steel pipe as barrel and receiver, welded or bolted steel plate for breech block, salvaged door hinge or angle iron as mounting points, steel bolt or nail as striker
physical_description.finish: Heavily oxidized and rust-streaked—bare steel with orange and brown corrosion patina, oil stains from repeated maintenance attempts, variable surface texture where welding bead is visible and rough
physical_description.color_scheme: Dull rust-orange and gunmetal gray with deep brown oxidation streaks; occasional smears of black grease or machine oil
physical_description.grip_texture: Bare welded steel or wrapped in degraded electrical tape, tire rubber strips, or clothesline cord—whatever provided traction. Rough and abrasive to the skin.
distinctive_features: Crude welds visible along pipe seams and breech connections, some cracked or incomplete
Misaligned breech block that sits at a slight angle, suggesting multiple rebuilds
Striker assembly fashioned from a heavy bolt or nail with a spring salvaged from a car door or bed frame
No sights beyond a filed notch in the pipe rim or welded-on nail stub
Shimming shims visible around the breach—bits of steel, aluminum, or even plastic wedged to adjust shell fit
Hand-stamped serial numbers or owner marks scratched or acid-etched into the pipe
Occasional copper or brass packing wadding visible at the muzzle from incomplete cleaning
Heat discoloration rings around the breech from repeated firing stress
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: No corporate branding. Typically bears hand-scratched owner tags, gang affiliations, or community fabrication marks (simple symbols, initials, or GLMZ sector codes) etched into the pipe near the breech
physical_description.condition_typical: Battle-worn and field-maintained. Surface corrosion is standard and expected; structural cracks or missing welds indicate imminent failure. Most examples show signs of hasty repairs—re-welded breech blocks, replacement strikers, new grip wrappings—suggesting regular fieldstripping and rebuilding by non-specialists.
